title: Smooth unipotent affine algebraic groups are solvable
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All group schemes below are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and all subgroup schemes are closed [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness is as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], and connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme]; geometrically connected means connected after extension to an algebraic closure $\bar k$ of $k$. A smooth affine group is unipotent if in a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation all its geometric points are unipotent matrices, meaning $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$. A group scheme is solvable if it has a finite descending series of closed subgroup schemes, each normal in its predecessor, with commutative group-scheme quotients. Every smooth unipotent group scheme $U$ over $k$ is solvable in this group-scheme sense, with no assumption that $k$ is perfect or has characteristic zero.

source.place: Proposition 14.21, first sentence of proof; Corollary 14.12 and Theorem 14.5.

proof.text: Here is the matrix calculation behind the standard series, grouped by superdiagonal distance. For each commutative $k$-algebra $R$ put $J_r(R)=\{A:A_{ij}=0\text{ unless }j-i\geq r\}$ for $1\leq r\leq n$. In matrix multiplication, a nonzero summand of $(AB)_{ij}$ requires $l-i\geq r$ and $j-l\geq s$; hence $J_rJ_s\subseteq J_{r+s}$, with $J_t=0$ for $t\geq n$. In the ring of upper triangular matrices each $J_r$ is a two-sided ideal. Thus $F_r(R)=I+J_r(R)$ is a subgroup: products use $A+B+AB$, and inverses use $I-A+A^2-\cdots+(-A)^{n-1}$. Each $F_r$ is closed, cut out by the entries of distance less than $r$. Reduction modulo $J_{r+1}$ shows $F_{r+1}(R)$ normal in $F_r(R)$ and $F_r(R)/F_{r+1}(R)$ commutative, since $J_rJ_r\subseteq J_{2r}\subseteq J_{r+1}$ for $r\geq1$. These identities hold for every $R$, including nonreduced $R$. Define $H_r\subseteq U$ by the same vanishing equations on $i(u)-I$. They give closed subgroup schemes by [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. The calculation gives $H_{r+1}\triangleleft H_r$ and $[x,y]\in H_{r+1}(R)$ for all $x,y\in H_r(R)$. Finally $H_1=U$ and $H_n=1$, since $i$ is a closed immersion.

source.place: Example 6.49, printed pp.136–137, equations (38) and (c), grouped by distance; Proposition 14.21, intersection construction. Explicit polynomial calculation supplied here.

proof.text: For $1\leq r<n$, apply [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] to $H_{r+1}\triangleleft H_r$: both are affine of finite type, as closed subschemes cut out by finitely many coordinate equations in the affine finite-type scheme $U$. It represents the fppf quotient $Q_r=H_r/H_{r+1}$ and makes $H_r\to Q_r$ locally surjective with kernel $H_{r+1}$. For $a,b\in Q_r(R)$ take a common fppf refinement on which both lift to $x,y\in H_r$. Step 2 puts $[x,y]$ in the kernel, so $ab=ba$ on that refinement and therefore over $R$ by the sheaf condition. This proves commutativity as a group scheme (the multiplication and its swapped multiplication agree on every algebra), as defined in [def-sc-group-scheme]. The finite series $U=H_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq H_n=1$ therefore proves the stated solvability. If $n=1$, it is the length-zero series of the trivial group.

source.place: Proposition 14.21, concluding sentence; normal quotients in Theorem 5.28 and Proposition 5.29, printed p.105, and sheaf interpretation in 5(j).
